text: Early lead: Q gives an exact surplus target and a measured failure of spread crossing in its double auction (Q, Market Environment and Trading Mechanism, lines 210-259; Results, lines 293-370). P converts LMM pairwise judgments into Bradley-Terry credits and potential-shaped rewards (P, Method, lines 281-350), but its convergence proposition only recovers the comparator latent preference, not economic contribution (P, lines 358-389). A concrete cross-paper test is whether rank-derived signals identify the action that closes a profitable spread and improve finite-horizon allocative efficiency in Q. I will check for a stronger analytical counterexample and whether the proposed shaping can actually change behavior under its policy-invariance guarantee.

Candidate bridge: Q gives a double auction with observable ex post total surplus and stalled spreads; P turns pairwise contribution judgments into scores and potential rewards. I am checking whether a welfare-grounded comparator could diagnose which agents cause missing trades, and whether P\(\,\)s policy-invariance property prevents the proposed shaping from fixing Q\(\,\)s strategic market failures. I will separate diagnosis from intervention and test an exact counterexample before recommending a publication question.

A concrete market-specific test for P: Q defines allocative efficiency as total buyer-plus-seller profit (Q §Results, lines 298–301) and gives private reservation prices (Q §Market Environment, lines 210–226). For one buyer value \(v\), seller cost \(c\), and any feasible transaction price \(p\), joint surplus is \((v-p)+(p-c)=v-c\). A two-person welfare coalition has Shapley credits \((v-c)/2\) each, independent of \(p\). Thus changing only the transaction price should not change welfare-credit rankings, though it reverses individual profit rankings when \(p\) crosses \((v+c)/2\). P §Rank Aggregation (lines 313–329) provides an LMM pairwise-comparison/Bradley–Terry pipeline whose welfare validity can be tested with this controlled nuisance intervention; P does not test transfer invariance. Next: determine what private information the comparator needs and whether shaping can affect the Q failure.

Independent analytical check: P defines unregularized Bradley-Terry MLE (P, Rank Aggregation, lines 313-329) and claims connected comparison graph suffices for finite-score recovery (P, Proposition and proof, lines 358-379, 677-748). It does not. With two agents and (K) unanimous comparisons favoring (i), the undirected graph is connected but (L(d)=K\log(1+e^{-d})), (d=c_i-c_j), has infimum only as (d\to\infty). Deterministic welfare labels in Q could generate precisely such separated data. Regularization/pseudocounts or a condition on bidirectional wins is needed before porting this ranker. This is distinct from the welfare/strategy issue and should be an explicit control, not the whole publication claim.

Correction to entry 4: the math delimiters were lost in command escaping. For two agents and \(K\) unanimous comparisons favoring \(i\), the connected comparison graph has unregularized Bradley-Terry loss \(L(d)=K\log(1+e^{-d})\), where \(d=c_i-c_j\). The infimum occurs only as \(d\to\infty\), so no finite MLE exists. A reciprocal win or explicit regularization is needed; mere undirected connectedness does not suffice.

Cross-check of #4: agreed. P §Rank Aggregation fits an unregularized Bradley–Terry objective; connectedness alone does not rule out separation. For the market test I would fit a penalized BT or add symmetric pseudocounts, and report separation frequency. This is important because exact welfare labels in Q can be deterministic. My distinct target is transfer invariance and identification: realized trade surplus cancels the transaction price, so a comparator must not confuse rent capture with welfare creation.

A simple P-to-Q intervention is not yet a publication claim. P analyzes cooperative team reward, while Q instructs each trader to maximize private profit (Q, Information and Objective, lines 261-278); in Q a transaction price transfers surplus between sides while total surplus stays \(v_b-v_s\). With P-style shaping \(F_{i,t}=\gamma\Phi_i(s_{t+1})-\Phi_i(s_t)\), fixed initial state and zero terminal potential, the discounted sum telescopes to \(-\Phi_i(s_0)\) for each agent, so exact policy-invariant shaping cannot remove a strategic inefficient equilibrium. It can change finite-sample learning, but Q freezes prompted LLM policies rather than training them. Also, adjacent prior work already uses an LLM critic to shape bidding in a continuous double auction: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18610 (fairness objective in electricity trading). A defensible novelty would need an economic ground-truth audit of P-style credits, not merely LLM-guided bidding.

A Q-specific boundary condition for P: Q removes both counterparties from the round immediately after a trade (Q, Trading Mechanism, lines 239-259). P computes softmax scores only over the active coalition and skips comparisons when fewer than two remain (P, lines 281-310, 331-349); it specifies zero potential for terminal states but does not spell out an exited agent potential (P, lines 331-349). For policy-invariant per-agent shaping, the exit transition must include \(\Phi_i(s_{t+1})=0\), or the inactive agent must continue receiving a defined potential, so that \(\sum_t\gamma^t F_{i,t}=-\Phi_i(s_0)\). If shaping is simply omitted after exit without an exit correction, the leftover potential depends on when the agent trades and can alter incentives. This is a testable implementation boundary; the text alone does not establish that P violates it.

Sharpened alternative to the generic crossing intervention: the right label is counterfactual final welfare, not whether an action crosses or yields immediate positive surplus. Q permits each buyer/seller one trade per round, with 300-iteration cap (Q, lines 239-259), and measures both missed and misallocated gains (Q, lines 293-302). Example using Q reservation grid: one seller has cost \(0.75\) and ask \(1.50\); buyer \(B_2\) values the good at \(2.25\), buyer \(B_1\) at \(3.25\). If \(B_2\) crosses now, welfare is \(2.25-0.75=1.50\); if it waits and \(B_1\) crosses later, welfare is \(3.25-0.75=2.50\). Thus crossing a profitable spread can lower final welfare by \(1.00\) through displacement, whereas near the deadline it may increase welfare if \(B_1\) will not arrive. P compares agents from contemporaneous observations (P, lines 281-310), so porting it to Q should compare candidate actions via paired rollouts under the same future random seed, with final allocative surplus as oracle. This makes the question dynamic and falsifiable: can LMM pairwise feedback predict the sign of the welfare difference across availability/horizon conditions?

I am changing the lead from “use P-style credit to make Q traders cross more” to “audit whether P-style pairwise judgments can rank quote actions by counterfactual final market welfare.” Q’s profitable crossing can either recover a missed trade or displace a higher-value trader (#9), and its private-profit objective differs from welfare (#7). The proposed study would replay Q states, compare a crossing quote with an incremental quote under matched future schedules/policies, label each pair by final surplus, and test LMM judgments under role swaps, price-only perturbations, and horizon changes. Penalized BT is a necessary implementation control because of #4–#6. I am checking whether this is distinguishable from existing auction/MARL work and whether the counterfactual protocol can respect Q’s information constraints.

Information-limit lemma for the proposed action benchmark: hold fixed Q-public history, seller cost \(0.75\), resting ask \(1.50\), and acting buyer \(B_2\) value \(2.25\). Let an unseen competing buyer \(B_1\) have value \(3.25\) in world A or \(1.75\) in world B; these are both Q-grid values and can yield the same public history. Suppose the same continuation has \(B_1\) cross later if \(B_2\) increments now. If \(B_2\) crosses now, welfare is \(1.50\) in either world. If \(B_2\) waits, welfare is \(2.50\) in A and \(1.00\) in B. Thus the welfare-preferred action reverses while \(B_2\)’s entire permitted information set can remain identical. A comparator restricted to Q’s trader information cannot perfectly label realized counterfactual welfare; evaluate its conditional expected welfare predictions separately from a privileged all-valuations oracle. This is a genuine cross-paper limitation of P’s image/observation-based comparisons (P, lines 281-310), not merely an LLM accuracy problem.

The #11 pair yields a sharper negative theorem than merely measuring judge accuracy: if the two hidden-value worlds occur with equal probability conditional on the same Q-permitted observation, any comparator measurable from that observation has accuracy at most \(1/2\) on the sign of \(Q^W(s,\mathrm{cross})-Q^W(s,\mathrm{increment})\). Increasing P’s comparison count \(K\) only concentrates estimates of this observation-conditioned preference; it cannot reveal the hidden buyer value. This distinguishes reducible LMM noise from structural non-identifiability. P explicitly frames rank aggregation as mitigating inaccuracies from partial observability (P, lines 351-379), but its bound targets recovery of the LMM latent preference, not true welfare contribution. An experiment should stratify by visibility: local trader information, paired agent information, and privileged all-valuations information; only the last can resolve this example. This is my strongest publication lead.

Correction to #12: “only the last can resolve this example” is too strong. A paired comparison that is allowed to read \(B_1\)’s private reservation value can also distinguish the two worlds; full-market access is sufficient but not necessary. The \(1/2\) ceiling applies specifically to a judge restricted to the acting trader’s information set (or any view that omits \(B_1\)’s value and has identical distributions across the worlds). The experiment must state which information regime each judge receives.

Decision-theoretic qualification to #12: a \(1/2\) ceiling on ex post pair-label accuracy under balanced hidden worlds is not a failure to choose the Bayes-optimal action. In that example, waiting has conditional expected welfare \((2.50+1.00)/2=1.75\), versus \(1.50\) for crossing, so a local judge could rationally always choose waiting while being wrong on half the realized-world labels. The experiment should report regret against both a conditional-information Bayes oracle and a privileged full-information oracle, with the gap between them identified as value of information. Repeated P comparisons can reduce judge variance but cannot close that information gap.

The same toy market quantifies the information gap: with equal probabilities for worlds A and B, the full-information oracle gets expected welfare \((2.50+1.50)/2=2.00\) by waiting in A and crossing in B; the best local policy gets \(1.75\) by waiting in both. Hence the value of seeing the competing buyer’s valuation is \(0.25\) surplus units. This is a fixed lower bound on what a local-information P-style evaluator can achieve in this constructed instance, irrespective of \(K\), assuming the stated continuation. It separates the structural limit from model quality.

Prior-work check narrows the novelty: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18610 already uses an LLM critic to shape bids in a continuous double auction; https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06859 already uses restored decision points and alternative-action rollouts for exact credit in cooperative LLM agents; https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.00285 studies Shapley counterfactual MARL credit. The possible new claim is specifically the information/welfare boundary for pairwise credit in a two-sided private-value market, plus a matched counterfactual audit of LMM judge rankings under Q’s observable-information rules. Search queries run: “multi agent reinforcement learning continuous double auction potential based reward shaping allocative efficiency”; “Bradley Terry rank aggregation credit assignment auction welfare multi agent language model”; “LLM double auction welfare feedback pairwise comparison market efficiency”; “counterfactual welfare credit assignment agent action double auction MARL paper”; “LLM judge pairwise action comparison social welfare double auction benchmark”; “comparison based reward shaping market auctions counterfactual welfare paper”. These results do not establish that the precise benchmark is novel.

Ada synthesis and proposed paper question: “When can pairwise LLM credit judgments identify welfare-improving quotes in a private-value double auction?” Q supplies a controlled \(22\)-trader market, exact ex post allocative surplus, a random offer schedule, and the observed failure mode of penny improvements instead of spread crossings (Q, Market Environment/Trading Mechanism, lines 210-259; Results, lines 293-370). Its prompt says each reservation price is known only to its holder (Q, Appendix Prompt Templates, lines 515-571). P supplies pairwise LMM comparisons, Bradley-Terry aggregation, and potential shaping, while its robustness claim recovers a latent comparator preference rather than proving alignment with welfare (P, Method/Theory, lines 281-389). The cross-paper result is the hidden-value construction #11–#15: the welfare-optimal quote action reverses across observationally identical worlds, yielding \(1/2\) ex post label accuracy at best and \(0.25\) expected surplus value of information under the stated balanced prior and continuation. Proposed test: sample Q decision states, compare a legal crossing quote against a legal incremental quote under matched exogenous schedules and fixed continuation policies, estimate final-surplus differences by repeated rollouts, then test judge/BT rankings and downstream welfare under local, paired-private, and full-information inputs. Report conditional-information Bayes regret separately from privileged-oracle regret; include price-only, role, and horizon perturbations, and regularize BT because #4–#6 show separation. No claim yet that this improves Q markets: exact potential shaping preserves equilibria when its telescoping conditions hold (#7–#8), and similar LLM-auction/LLM-counterfactual methods exist (#16). Open issues: empirical effect size, feasible cost of rollout labels, whether Q’s LLM policies are stable enough for matched continuation, and whether pairwise judging adds value over direct welfare regression. This is the best supported line I find.

Cross-check of #11–#17: Q fixes one buyer at each reservation value on the \(\$0.75\)–\(\$3.25\) grid (Q lines 210–226), so changing \(B_1\) from \(3.25\) to \(1.75\) must be implemented by swapping its valuation with an otherwise unseen buyer, preserving the fixed demand schedule. The two worlds can then share the same public history if neither swapped buyer has posted. Also P compares *agents* at a state (P lines 281–329), whereas the proposed benchmark compares two *actions of the same agent*. That is a defensible adaptation but must be stated as such; P’s BT score alone does not produce counterfactual quote rankings. A study should include direct local-information expected-welfare prediction as a baseline, since privileged full-information welfare is arithmetically available from Q’s values and allocations.

Sharpening the hidden-value experiment: preserve Q’s exact 11-value buyer multiset by swapping the values \(3.25\) and \(1.75\) between unseen buyers \(B_1\) and \(B_3\), while the acting buyer has \(v_2=2.25\) and the sole relevant resting ask is \(a^*=1.50\) from a seller with cost \(0.75\). Compare a legal crossing bid \(1.50\) with a legal improving bid \(1.49\), and couple the continuation so \(B_1\) is selected next and crosses if the seller remains. Final surplus differences are \(1.50-2.50=-1.00\) in the first world and \(1.50-1.00=+0.50\) in the second. The remaining buyer \(B_3\) must not trade before the horizon; e.g., use a near-cap decision. Conditional on equal-probability worlds, the local Bayes action is to wait, with expected welfare \(1.75\); the full-information policy obtains \(2.00\), an information value of \(0.25\). This is a constructed admissible continuation, not an observed Q trajectory. Randomize value-to-identity assignments and control prior public histories, or identity/history leakage could destroy the observational equivalence. Q’s private-profit prompt (lines 515–527) means welfare feedback alone gives no reason to expect a self-interested trader to adopt the welfare action.

I accept emmy #19. Q fixes the 11-buyer reservation-value multiset on the \(\$0.75\)-to-\(\$3.25\) grid (Q, Market Environment, lines 210-226), so worlds A and B swap \(B_1\)'s values \(3.25\) and \(1.75\) with an otherwise unseen buyer \(B_3\); they cannot change aggregate demand. A clean finite-horizon instance takes a legal state just before the acting buyer \(B_2\)'s turn, with one later iteration left, seller cost \(0.75\), sole standing ask \(1.50\), \(B_2\) value \(2.25\), and a lower standing bid. Condition on the same random schedule selecting \(B_1\) for the final turn, with \(B_3\) unselected and both swapped buyers absent from the public history. If \(B_1\) crosses the ask when available under the stipulated continuation, crossing now gives welfare \(1.50\); incrementing below the ask gives final welfare \(2.50\) in A and \(1.00\) in B. This is an existence example under an explicit continuation, not a claim about frequencies under Q's LLM policies. Q, Trading Mechanism, lines 239-259 and Information and Objective, lines 261-278, make the actions and information restriction precise. Also P, LMM-based Pairwise Comparison/Rank Aggregation, lines 281-329, compares agents' contributions, not alternative actions by one agent. The proposed quote-action comparison is an adaptation of its pairwise-judgment idea; P's BT agent scores alone do not rank the two quotes.

Cross-check of emmy #3 and #20: the price-cancellation identity \((v-p)+(p-c)=v-c\) establishes transfer invariance only conditional on the same matched trade/allocation. A changed quote or transaction price can alter later bids and hence final welfare through Q's auction dynamics (Q, Trading Mechanism, lines 239-259). Therefore the proposed price-only control should freeze the allocation and continuation when testing whether a judge mistakes rent capture for welfare; a separate perturbation can allow endogenous responses and measure total causal effect. For the main benchmark, pairwise quote ranking is an explicit extension of P, and two candidate quotes need no Bradley-Terry fit. Use P-style repeated pairwise judgments and rank aggregation only if testing a larger legal quote set; compare against direct predicted conditional expected welfare as a baseline. P's own limitations say tasks with domain-specific internal states unavailable to observations may lie outside scope (P, Limitations, lines 642 onward), which tempers any novelty claim about the hidden-value boundary.

I accept ada #22 and have checked the construction against Q and P. The fixed buyer-value multiset is preserved by swapping values of unseen buyers, and the quote pair is legal when the standing bid is below \(1.49\). The sign reversal and \(0.25\) value-of-information calculation require the stated final-turn selection and continuation, so they are an existence result, not a frequency claim about Q agents. I wrote the full derivation and falsifiable test in emmy/market-credit-note.md. Crucial distinction: P compares agents, while quote-action comparisons adapt its judgment method; a direct conditional-welfare predictor is the baseline. Remaining publication requirements are measured state frequency and predictive advantage over that baseline.

I accept ada #23. The price-cancellation identity applies to a fixed matched trade and continuation; changing a quote may alter later behavior and therefore final welfare. The note emmy/market-credit-note.md now specifies an allocation-fixed price diagnostic versus an endogenous-response causal test. It also says two candidate quotes need direct pairwise judgment only; Bradley-Terry aggregation is an optional extension for a larger quote set. P Limitations (lines 642-646) already flags hidden domain-specific state as a scope limit, so the proposed contribution is a quantified private-value market boundary and empirical audit, not a contradiction of P.

Cross-check after emmy #25: Q selects the next actor uniformly among agents who have not transacted (Q, Trading Mechanism, lines 241-259), so crossing removes \(B_2\) and \(S\) and changes the next-turn choice set. A paired-rollout protocol should couple the underlying random priority/draws, then apply Q selection separately in each branch; it should not force an identical selected-agent sequence, which can change probabilities. The constructed final-turn example remains admissible by conditioning on a coupled draw that selects \(B_1\) in both branches. The label reversal and \(0.25\) information value are conditional on that continuation, not unconditional estimates for Q. At iteration 299, two unseen buyers is also likely rare; replay data should measure support for comparable states rather than treat the example as typical. P explicitly places unobserved domain-specific states outside its current scope (P, Limitations, lines 640-642), so this is a quantified boundary and benchmark proposal, not a refutation.
